title: Four Names Behind the First Insulin

scenes.tts: The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and, in islets, a hormone. By 1920, extracts lowered blood sugar, but none was safe for patients. In November 1920, Frederick Banting took an idea to John Macleod, a Toronto professor. Tie off the pancreatic duct in dogs. The enzyme-making tissue wastes away. Extract what is left.
scenes.visual: A pancreas blob with enzyme tissue and gold islet dots; extracts that lower blood sugar are crossed out as unsafe; Banting takes the idea to Macleod; the duct is tied and the enzyme tissue shrinks, leaving islets.
scenes.narration: The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and, in islets, a hormone. By 1920, extracts lowered blood sugar, but none was safe for patients. In November 1920, Frederick Banting took an idea to John Macleod, a Toronto professor. Tie off the pancreatic duct in dogs. The enzyme-making tissue wastes away. Extract what is left.

scenes.tts: Macleod gave space, dogs, and two student assistants. One was Charles Best. In summer 1921, Banting and Best made extracts that lowered blood sugar in diabetic dogs. On 11 January 1922, their extract went into Leonard Thompson, then in his early teens. His blood sugar fell a little, and an abscess formed.
scenes.visual: Macleod hands over three things; one of two assistant chips becomes Charles Best; Banting and Best make an extract that lowers a dog's blood sugar; Leonard Thompson's blood sugar dips a little and an abscess is flagged.

scenes.tts: The extract was too impure. James Collip raised the alcohol concentration in steps. Impurities dropped out of solution, while the active substance stayed in. He tested each batch on rabbits. It went into the same boy on 23 January. His blood sugar fell by about three quarters.
scenes.visual: A beaker holds gold active dots and grey impurities; alcohol steps rise and grey dots settle out while gold stay; each batch goes to rabbits; Thompson's blood sugar falls far on 23 January.
scenes.narration: The extract was too impure. James Collip raised the alcohol concentration in steps. Impurities dropped out of solution, while the active substance stayed in. He tested each batch on rabbits. It went into the same boy on 23 January. His blood sugar fell by about three quarters.

scenes.tts: The 1923 Nobel Prize named Banting and Macleod. Banting shared his prize money with Best, Macleod with Collip. The two-name story misses half the people. The receptor was not known to be a tyrosine kinase until 1982. The drug came first, and the mechanism came later.
scenes.visual: Banting and Macleod under a 1923 Nobel label; prize money arrows to Best and Collip; four people shown; a drug chip stands beside an empty mechanism box until the 1982 tick.
